title: Monitor pests, diseases and weeds on crops

lessons.title: Scouting and trapping pests
lessons.html:
Why we scout

Scouting means walking through a crop in a planned way to look for pests, diseases and weeds. Good scouting finds problems early, when they are still cheap and easy to control. It also stops unnecessary spraying, because you only spray when the numbers show it is needed.

Know the common pests of your enterprise

CropCommon pests
MaizeFall armyworm, stalk borers, cutworms, aphids
TomatoesTuta absoluta (tomato leafminer), bollworm, whitefly, red spider mite
CabbageDiamondback moth, aphids, cabbage webworm
CitrusFalse codling moth, thrips, scale insects, fruit fly

Learn the life stages of each pest (egg, larva or nymph, pupa, adult) and where they hide on the plant. Also learn to recognise beneficial insects such as ladybirds, lacewings and parasitic wasps, so they are not counted as pests.

A scouting method

  1. Use the same pattern every time, for example a W or zig-zag across the land, so the whole land is sampled.
  2. Stop at a set number of points and inspect a set number of plants at each point.
  3. Check the top and underside of leaves, growing points, stems, flowers and fruit.
  4. Count the pests and beneficials and note the growth stage of the crop.
  5. Record on the scouting sheet before moving on.

Traps

  • Pheromone traps attract male moths of one species (for example bollworm, false codling moth or Tuta). Weekly counts show when a flight starts.
  • Yellow sticky traps catch whiteflies, aphids and leafminers in tunnels.
  • Fruit fly traps with bait or lures in orchards.

Number every trap, mark it on the map, check it on a fixed day each week, record the count, and replace lures and sticky cards as the supplier recommends.

lessons.title: Monitoring diseases and collecting specimens
lessons.html:
Recognising disease symptoms

Plant diseases are caused by fungi, bacteria and viruses. You see the symptoms, not the organism itself.

SymptomExample
Leaf spots or blightEarly and late blight on tomatoes and potatoes, grey leaf spot on maize
Rust (orange or brown powdery pustules)Wheat rust, bean rust
Powdery white growthPowdery mildew on cucurbits and grapes
Wilting with brown stem insideFusarium or bacterial wilt
Mottled, curled or yellow leaves, stuntingVirus diseases, often spread by aphids or whiteflies
Rots on fruit or rootsMany fungi and bacteria, often after wet weather

Weather is important: many fungal diseases spread fast in warm, humid or wet conditions. Scout more often after rain.

Recording disease

  • Note the symptom, the part of the plant, the percentage of plants affected and where in the land (patches, edges, low spots).
  • Take a clear photo of the symptom, close up and of the whole plant.

Collecting specimens you do not recognise

  1. Collect insects in a clean container or vial; use a soft brush. Soft-bodied insects can be stored in alcohol if your adviser asks for this.
  2. For diseases, take whole affected plants or plant parts showing early and advanced symptoms; wrap in dry newspaper and put in a plastic bag.
  3. Label with date, farm, land, crop, collector and what you saw.
  4. Keep cool and deliver quickly to your supervisor, adviser or a diagnostic laboratory.
  5. Record the identification when it comes back so you know it next time.

Wash your hands after handling diseased material, and do not walk from an infected land into a clean one without cleaning boots where the farm requires it.

lessons.title: Weeds, recording and reporting
lessons.html:
Monitoring weeds

Weeds compete with the crop for water, light and nutrients, host pests and diseases, and make harvesting harder. Some are declared weeds or invader plants that must be controlled under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983.

  • Learn the main weeds on the farm: grasses (such as crabfinger grass, nutgrass) and broadleaf weeds (such as pigweed, blackjack, thorn apple).
  • Record the weed species, growth stage (seedling, flowering, seeding) and density (few, moderate, dense) for each land.
  • Note weeds that survived herbicide applications; this can point to resistance or poor application.
  • Note new weeds that have not been seen on the farm before.

Recording and reporting

A good scouting sheet includes

  • Date, scout's name, land, crop and growth stage.
  • Pests and beneficials counted per sampling point.
  • Disease symptoms and percentage affected.
  • Weed species and density.
  • Trap counts.
  • Weather conditions.

Turning records into recommendations

Compare the counts with the action thresholds supplied by your crop adviser. Example: if the threshold for a pest is reached at 10% of plants infested and your count shows 4 of 50 plants (8%), keep monitoring; if next week's count is 8 of 50 (16%), recommend control to your manager. Mention the area affected, the pest stage and whether beneficial insects are present.

Report straight away if you find a pest that is new to the area or a suspected quarantine pest, so the farm can contact the Department of Agriculture.

Key points

  • Scout in a fixed pattern with a fixed sample size and record at each point.
  • Learn pests, beneficials and their life stages.
  • Check traps on a fixed day and record counts.
  • Collect and label unknown insects and diseased plants for identification.
  • Compare counts with thresholds and give clear recommendations.
